steps.stem:
The operation \(\blacklozenge\) is defined for every number \(a\): \(\blacklozenge(a)=a^2-4a\)
\(\blacklozenge(6)=?\)

The operation \(\blacklozenge\) is defined for every number \(x\): \(\blacklozenge(x)=x^2\)
\(\blacklozenge(\blacklozenge(3))=?\)
Given: \(\blacklozenge(3)=21\). Which of the following cannot be the definition of the operation \(\blacklozenge\)?
explanation: Put \(x=3\) into each choice. A choice that does not give \(21\) cannot be the definition.

steps.stem:
For every number \(x\): \(\blacklozenge(x)=x^2-2x\)
\(\blacklozenge(x+1)=?\)
explanation: Put \(x+1\) where \(x\) was — in brackets, every time: \(\blacklozenge(x+1)=(x+1)^2-2(x+1)\).
The traps: \(\blacklozenge(x)+1=x^2-2x+1\) (choice 1), \((x+1)^2\) written as \(x^2+1\) (choice 3), and \(-2(x+1)\) written as \(-2x+2\) (choice 4).

steps.stem: For which of the following operations is \(a\star b=b\star a\) for all numbers \(a\) and \(b\)?
explanation: To show "not always", one counterexample is enough. Take \(a=1\) and \(b=2\) (different, and not \(0\)).
(3) To show "always", swap the letters in the algebra: \(b\star a=ba+b+a=ab+a+b=a\star b\) ✓.
Do not test with \(a=b\): then both sides are \(a\star a\) for every operation.

steps.title: New operations — what to do
steps.intro: Read the definition first. Then follow it exactly.

head: Type
What to do
Example
rows: substitute the input for every letter
first turn each operation into a number
put the given input into each choice
equation — or work back from the answers
not always: one counterexample; always: swap the letters
check odd / even at every step
try every rule; keep an answer only if it fits its rule
down to the start value, then back up
only the odd powers are left, doubled
put each rule on trial with a test value (not \(0\) or \(1\)) · a step property: two neighbors
undo the steps in reverse order, then check with a number
skip, come back last, plug in

tips: A new operation need not behave like plus: \(2\star4\ne4\star2\).
Plugging in: avoid \(0\), \(1\) and equal values — they can make a false rule look true. If two choices survive, try a second number.

steps.stem:
The operation \(\blacklozenge\) is defined for every number \(x\): \(\blacklozenge(2x)=x+5\)
\(\blacklozenge(14)=?\)
explanation: The input of \(\blacklozenge\) is \(2x\), not \(x\). So find the \(x\) with \(2x=14\): \(x=7\).
The trap: putting \(14\) straight into \(x+5\) gives \(19\).

steps.stem:
The operation \(\blacklozenge\) is defined for every integer \(x\):
\(\blacklozenge(x)=\begin{cases} 2x, & x \text{ odd} \\ x^2-3, & x \text{ even} \end{cases}\)
\(\blacklozenge(\blacklozenge(\blacklozenge(3)))=?\)
explanation: Check odd or even again before every step.

steps.stem:
The operation \(\blacklozenge\) is defined for every positive integer \(x\):
\(\blacklozenge(x)=\begin{cases} 3x, & x \text{ odd} \\ x^2-12, & x \text{ even} \end{cases}\)
Given: \(\blacklozenge(x)=24\)
\(x=?\)
explanation: Try both rules, then check that each answer fits the rule it used.
Odd rule: \(3x=24\), so \(x=8\). But \(8\) is even, so it does not use the odd rule. Rejected.
Even rule: \(x^2-12=24\), so \(x^2=36\) and \(x=6\) (\(x\) is positive). \(6\) is even ✓.

steps.stem:
The operation \(\blacklozenge\) is defined for every even integer \(x\ge0\):
\(\blacklozenge(x)=\begin{cases} 2, & x=0 \\ 9-\blacklozenge(x-2), & x\ge2 \end{cases}\)
\(\blacklozenge(6)=?\)
explanation: Go down to the start value: \(\blacklozenge(6)=9-\blacklozenge(4)\), \(\blacklozenge(4)=9-\blacklozenge(2)\), \(\blacklozenge(2)=9-\blacklozenge(0)\), and \(\blacklozenge(0)=2\).
The values go \(2, 7, 2, 7\) — they switch back and forth.

steps.stem:
The operation \(\blacklozenge\) is defined for every positive integer \(x\):
\(\blacklozenge(x)=\begin{cases} 9, & x=1 \\ \blacklozenge(x-1), & x>1 \end{cases}\)
\(\blacklozenge(7)=?\)
explanation: Each value copies the one below it, so the start value \(9\) passes all the way up.

steps.stem:
For every number \(x\): \(5\cdot\blacklozenge(x)-3x=8+4\cdot\blacklozenge(x)\)
\(\blacklozenge(4)=?\)
explanation: Treat \(\blacklozenge(x)\) as one unknown and isolate it: \(5\cdot\blacklozenge(x)-4\cdot\blacklozenge(x)=8+3x\), so \(\blacklozenge(x)=3x+8\).

steps.stem: For every number \(t\): \(\blacklozenge(t)=t^2\). In the choices, \(x\ge0\). Which of the following is not always true?
explanation: (3) \(\blacklozenge(5x)=(5x)^2=25x^2\), but \(5\cdot\blacklozenge(x)=5x^2\). With \(x=1\): \(25\ne5\). Not always true — this is the answer.
(2) \(\blacklozenge(\sqrt x)=(\sqrt x)^2=x\), so \(\blacklozenge(\blacklozenge(\sqrt x))=\blacklozenge(x)\). Always true.
(4) Opposite numbers have the same square, so \((x-2)^2=(2-x)^2\). Always true.
Plugging in? Do not use \(x=0\): with \(x=0\) every choice looks true.

steps.stem:
The operation \(\blacklozenge\) is defined for every positive number \(x\).
It is known that for every positive \(x\): \(\blacklozenge(\blacklozenge(x))=x\).
Which of the following can be the definition of the operation \(\blacklozenge\)?
explanation: Put each rule on trial with \(x=2\): apply it twice and see if you get back to \(2\).
\(\frac{c}{x}\) always undoes itself. \(\frac{x}{6}\) looks similar, but it keeps getting smaller.

steps.stem:
For every three numbers \(x\), \(y\), \(z\): \(\blacklozenge(x, y, z)=x^{yz}+y^{xz}+z^{xy}\)
\(\blacklozenge(1, 1, \blacklozenge(2, 1, 3))=?\)

For every two numbers \(x\) and \(y\), two operations are defined:
\(\begin{cases} \blacklozenge(x, y)=x^2-2xy+y^2 \\ \#(x, y)=x^2+2xy+y^2 \end{cases}\)
\(\#(\blacklozenge(10, 6), \blacklozenge(5, 4))=?\)
explanation: Recognize the square formulas: \(\blacklozenge(x, y)=(x-y)^2\) and \(\#(x, y)=(x+y)^2\).

steps.stem:
For every number \(x\): \(\blacklozenge(x)=x^5+3x^4-2x^3+x^2+4x-7\)
\(\blacklozenge(2)-\blacklozenge(-2)=?\)
explanation: Shortcut: an even power, and the constant, give the same value for \(2\) and \(-2\), so they cancel in the subtraction. An odd power only changes its sign, so it is doubled.
Only the odd terms are left: \(2\cdot(2^5-2\cdot2^3+4\cdot2)=2\cdot(32-16+8)=2\cdot24=48\).
The trap \(90\) is \(\blacklozenge(2)+\blacklozenge(-2)\) — there only the even terms survive: \(2\cdot(48+4-7)=90\).

steps.stem:
For every two numbers \(x\) and \(y\): \(\blacklozenge(x, y)=\sqrt{8x^2+y^2}\). Given: \(a>0\)
\(\frac{\blacklozenge(\blacklozenge(a, a), a)}{\blacklozenge(a, \blacklozenge(a, a))}=?\)
explanation: Top: \(3a\) goes into the FIRST slot: \(\blacklozenge(3a, a)=\sqrt{8\cdot9a^2+a^2}=\sqrt{73a^2}=a\sqrt{73}\).
Bottom: \(3a\) goes into the SECOND slot: \(\blacklozenge(a, 3a)=\sqrt{8a^2+9a^2}=\sqrt{17a^2}=a\sqrt{17}\).

steps.stem:
For every two numbers \(x\) and \(y\) that are not \(0\): \(\blacklozenge(x, y)=\frac{(x-y)^2}{xy^3}\). Given: \(a\) and \(b\) are two different numbers, and neither of them is \(0\).
\(\frac{\blacklozenge(a, b)}{\blacklozenge(b, a)}=?\)
explanation: The tops are equal, because \((b-a)^2=(a-b)^2\). They cancel:

steps.stem: \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) are digits from \(1\) to \(9\). For every three-digit number \(ABC\), the operation \(\blacklozenge\) is defined: \(\blacklozenge(ABC)=A^4+B^3+C^2\). Which of the following is the smallest?
explanation: The smallest is \(\blacklozenge(124)=25\): the biggest power goes on the smallest digit.

steps.stem: For every number \(x\ne0\): \(\blacklozenge(x)=\frac3x\). Which of the following must be true for all positive \(a\) and \(b\)?
explanation: (2) \(\blacklozenge(a)\cdot a=\frac3a\cdot a=3\) and \(\blacklozenge(b)\cdot b=\frac3b\cdot b=3\). Both sides are always \(3\) ✓.
(1) \(a=\frac12\) gives \(\blacklozenge(a)=6\), which is not less than \(3\) ✗.
(4) A bigger denominator gives a smaller fraction: \(\frac3a>\frac3{a+1}\). For example \(a=1\): \(3>\frac32\) ✗.

steps.stem: For every positive integer \(x\), ⟦\(x\)⟧ is the number of times \(5\) appears in the prime factorization of \(x\). For example, \(50=2\cdot5\cdot5\) has two 5s, so ⟦\(50\)⟧ is \(2\). Which of the following must be true?
explanation: Multiplying \(x\) by \(5\) adds exactly one more \(5\) to its prime factorization. So ⟦\(5x\)⟧ \(=\) ⟦\(x\)⟧ \(+1\) always ✓.

steps.stem:
For every two numbers \(a\) and \(b\): \(a\star b=2a-b\)
\(3\star5=?\)

For every two numbers \(a\) and \(b\): \(a\circ b=(a-b)^2\)
\((-2)\circ3=?\)

Given:
\(\begin{cases} G(x)=2x+5 \text{ for every number } x \\ G(t)=19 \end{cases}\)
\(t=?\)

For every two different numbers \(x\) and \(y\), two operations are defined:
\(\blacklozenge(x, y)\) = the smaller of \(x\) and \(y\)
\(\#(x, y)\) = the larger of \(x\) and \(y\)
\(\#(\blacklozenge(8, 5), \blacklozenge(12, 2))=?\)

For all \(a\) and \(b\) with \(a\ge b\ge0\): \(\blacklozenge(a, b)=\sqrt{\sqrt a-\sqrt b}\)
\(\frac{\blacklozenge(169, 16)}{\blacklozenge(36, 25)}=?\)

For every two numbers \(x\) and \(y\): \(\blacklozenge(x, y)=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\)
\(\blacklozenge(\blacklozenge(4, 1), 8)=?\)

For every number \(x\): \(\blacklozenge(x)=x(x-3)\)
\(\blacklozenge(\blacklozenge(4))=?\)
explanation: Outer: \(\blacklozenge(4)=4\) again. The operation sends \(4\) back to \(4\).

steps.stem:
For every number \(x\): \(\blacklozenge(x)=2x^2-x\)
\(\blacklozenge(x-1)=?\)
explanation: Check with \(x=2\): \(\blacklozenge(1)=2-1=1\), and \(8-10+3=1\) ✓. The other choices give \(-1\), \(5\) and \(5\).

steps.stem:
For every number \(a\): \(\blacklozenge(a^2)=|a|\)
\(\blacklozenge\left(\frac1{16}\right)=?\)
explanation: The input is \(a^2\). Find \(a\) with \(a^2=\frac1{16}\): \(a=\frac14\) or \(a=-\frac14\).

steps.stem:
For every number \(x\): \(\blacklozenge(x)+2=10x-\blacklozenge(x)\)
\(\blacklozenge(3)=?\)

For every positive integer \(n\):
\(\blacklozenge(n)=\begin{cases} 7, & n=1 \\ \blacklozenge(n-1)+3, & n>1 \end{cases}\)
\(\blacklozenge(5)=?\)
explanation: Climb up from the start value: \(\blacklozenge(1)=7\), \(\blacklozenge(2)=10\), \(\blacklozenge(3)=13\), \(\blacklozenge(4)=16\), \(\blacklozenge(5)=19\).
Or: four steps of \(+3\) above the start value: \(7+4\cdot3=19\).

steps.stem:
For every two numbers \(a\) and \(b\):
\(a\blacklozenge b=\begin{cases} \frac{a+b}{a-b}, & a\ne b \\ 0, & a=b \end{cases}\)
\((5\blacklozenge3)\blacklozenge4=?\)
explanation: Outer: \(4\blacklozenge4\) has \(a=b\), so the second rule gives \(0\).

steps.stem:
For every positive integer \(a\): \(\blacklozenge(a)=\frac{a}{a+1}\)
\(\blacklozenge(2)\cdot\blacklozenge(3)\cdot\blacklozenge(4)\cdot\blacklozenge(5)\cdot\blacklozenge(6)\cdot\blacklozenge(7)=?\)
explanation: Each top cancels the bottom before it: \(3\), \(4\), \(5\), \(6\) and \(7\) all cancel. What is left: \(\frac28=\frac14\).
The trap \(\frac18\) forgets that the product starts at \(\blacklozenge(2)\), so the first top is \(2\), not \(1\).

steps.stem: For every number \(x\): \(\blacklozenge(x)=x(x+5)(x-2)\). For how many different values of \(x\) is \(\blacklozenge(x)\) equal to \(0\)?
explanation: A product is \(0\) exactly when one of its factors is \(0\): \(x=0\), or \(x+5=0\), or \(x-2=0\).

steps.stem:
For every two positive integers \(a\) and \(b\), \(\blacklozenge(a, b)\) is the remainder when \(a\) is divided by \(b\).
\(\blacklozenge(\blacklozenge(38, 7), \blacklozenge(23, 6))=?\)
explanation: \(\blacklozenge(3, 5)\): \(3=0\cdot5+3\), so the remainder is \(3\). (A smaller number divided by a bigger one leaves itself.)

steps.stem:
For every integer \(n\) from \(1\) to \(9\), \(\blacklozenge(n)\) is the number of two-digit numbers whose tens digit is \(n\) and whose units digit is smaller than \(n\).
\(\blacklozenge(n)=?\)
explanation: Examples first. \(n=4\): the numbers \(40\), \(41\), \(42\), \(43\). Four numbers, so \(\blacklozenge(4)=4\).
In general, the units digit can be \(0, 1, \ldots, n-1\): that is \(n\) digits. So \(\blacklozenge(n)=n\).

steps.stem:
For every number \(a\): \(\blacklozenge(a)=a^5+a^4+a^3+a^2+a+1\)
\(\blacklozenge(1)-\blacklozenge(-1)=?\)
explanation: Shortcut: in \(\blacklozenge(1)-\blacklozenge(-1)\) the even powers and the constant cancel. Only the \(3\) odd powers are left, doubled: \(2\cdot3=6\).

steps.stem:
For every number \(x\): \(\blacklozenge(x)=x^4+2x^2+7x-5\)
\(\blacklozenge(3)-\blacklozenge(-3)=?\)
explanation: Shortcut: the even powers and the constant are the same for \(3\) and \(-3\), so they cancel. Only \(7x\) is left, doubled: \(2\cdot7\cdot3=42\).

steps.stem:
The operation \(\blacklozenge\) is defined for every integer \(x\):
\(\blacklozenge(x)=\begin{cases} x^2-5, & x\ge0 \\ -2x, & x<0 \end{cases}\)
For how many integers \(x\) is \(\blacklozenge(x)\) equal to \(4\)?
explanation: Try both rules, and keep only answers that fit their rule.
First rule: \(x^2-5=4\), so \(x^2=9\): \(x=3\) or \(x=-3\). This rule is only for \(x\ge0\), so keep \(x=3\) and reject \(x=-3\).

steps.stem:
For every two integers \(a\) and \(b\) that are not \(0\): \(\blacklozenge(a, b)=\frac{a}{b}-\frac{b}{a}\)
\(\blacklozenge(-1, 3)=?\)

For every number \(x\), two operations are defined:
\(\begin{cases} \blacklozenge(x)=x+5 \\ \#(x)=x^2 \end{cases}\)
Given: \(\blacklozenge(\#(a))=\#(\blacklozenge(a))\)
\(a=?\)
For every number \(x\): \(\blacklozenge(x)=(x-4)(x+1)\). For how many values of \(a\) is \(\blacklozenge(a)\) equal to \(\blacklozenge(a+4)\)?
explanation: \(a^2-3a-4=a^2+5a\): the \(a^2\) cancels, so \(-4=8a\) and \(a=-\frac12\). Exactly one value.

steps.stem:
The operation \(\blacklozenge\) is defined for every positive integer \(x\).
It is known that for every positive integer \(x\): \(\blacklozenge(x+1)=\blacklozenge(x)+3\).
Which of the following can be the definition of the operation \(\blacklozenge\)?
explanation: A step property: test two neighbors, \(x=2\) and \(x=3\). The second result must be \(3\) more than the first.
In general: \(3(x+1)=3x+3\) ✓. The trap is choice 1: "plus \(3\)" in the property does not mean "plus \(3\)" in the rule.

steps.stem:
The operation \(\#\) is the inverse operation of \(\blacklozenge\). For every positive number \(x\):
\(\begin{cases} \blacklozenge(x)=\sqrt{x}+4 \\ \#(\blacklozenge(x))=x \end{cases}\)
What is \(\#(y)\)?
explanation: The steps of \(\blacklozenge\): first take the root, then add \(4\).
Undo them in reverse order: first subtract \(4\), then square. \(\#(y)=(y-4)^2\).
Check with \(x=9\): \(\blacklozenge(9)=3+4=7\), and \(\#(7)=(7-4)^2=9\) ✓. The other choices give \(45\), \(\sqrt7-4\) and \(121\).
Choice 1 undoes the steps in the wrong order.

steps.stem: For two positive integers \(x\) and \(y\), \(x\sim y\) is the number you get when you write the digits of \(x\) and then the digits of \(y\). For example: \(36\sim7=367\). Which of the following is not always true for positive integers \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\)?
explanation: One counterexample is enough: \(36\sim7=367\), but \(7\sim36=736\). So (1) is not always true.

The others are always true. (2) \(2\sim x\) has one more digit than \(x\), so it is bigger. (3) Writing the digit \(3\) after \(x\) moves every digit of \(x\) one place to the left and adds \(3\): for example \(58\sim3=583=10\cdot58+3\). (4) Both sides are the digits of \(x\), then \(y\), then \(z\), in that order.

steps.stem: For every number \(x\ne0\): \(\blacklozenge(x)=\frac{x-3}{x}\). Which of the following must be true for all \(a>3\) and \(b>3\)?
explanation: (3) Two numbers between \(0\) and \(1\) have a product smaller than \(1\). Always true ✓.
(1) As \(x\) grows, \(\frac3x\) shrinks, so \(\blacklozenge(x)\) grows: \(a<b\) gives \(\blacklozenge(a)<\blacklozenge(b)\). The claim is the reverse ✗.

steps.stem: For every number \(x\): \(\blacklozenge(x)=x^2-9\). Given: \(a>0\) and \(b>0\). Which of the following must be true?
explanation: (2) Left side: \(\sqrt{a^2-9+9}=\sqrt{a^2}=a\) (\(a\) is positive). Right side: \(\frac{a^2-9}{a+3}+3=\frac{(a-3)(a+3)}{a+3}+3=a-3+3=a\). Always equal ✓.
